item.title: Rescuing Picture Quality on a Weak Network: What Receiver-Side "Low-Res to HD" Can Actually Do
item.description:
A chain store’s cameras report over 4G; during the evening rush the picture smears into mush. A construction-site camera doesn’t have the uplink; the license plate in the recording is never legible. After reading a product brochure, the owner asks a natural question: AI can sharpen old photos now — can it sharpen my footage too?

The question deserves a real answer, because it isn’t a yes or a no. In October 2026 I traced this line from papers and open-source projects through commercial products to court rulings. The conclusion up front: receiver-side super-resolution helps with exactly one specific damage class; it cannot fix corruption or stutter; and in surveillance/forensics contexts it carries a legal red line. This post explains why, written for readers with no video-coding background — every term is explained where it first appears.

item.title: Omni-Modal AI Interaction Survey: Vision, Audio, Dialogue, and Task Execution
item.description: A 2024 GPT-4o demo — talking while listening, interruptible mid-sentence — turned omni-modal interaction from a paper keyword into a product direction. Two years on, the industry has split into two implementation routes: one stuffs listening, seeing, and speaking into a single end-to-end model (Omni models); the other chains VAD, ASR, LLM, and TTS into a pipeline. This post walks through both routes’ technical approaches, maturity, and representative open-source projects. Facts verified as of October 2026.

item.title: Who Speaks, Who They Mean, Whether to Answer: Response Decision in Voice Dialogue
item.description:
The previous survey had a section on “how a conversation starts” comparing wake words with other entry points. This post goes one layer deeper: what does the wake word actually do for the system, and what has to replace it when you remove it?

The answer is three judgments. When you call “Hey XiaoAi” at a speaker, the system instantly settles three things: whoever says the name is probably an enrolled user (who is speaking); the name is aimed at the device (who they’re talking to); a name obviously deserves a reply (whether to answer). Human conversation never starts every sentence with a name, because the human brain runs these three judgments continuously in the background — recognizing voices, working out whether a remark is aimed at you, deciding when to chime in and when to just listen.

item.title: Can Vision Models Read Images and Watch Video? A Capability Survey: What's Solved and What's an Industry-Wide Boundary
item.description:
Suppose you’re handed a requirement: ten thousand hours of surveillance footage, and it must answer two kinds of questions. Kind one: “Who is this person,” “where did this car go,” “when did he enter the server room.” Kind two: “What was he doing in there,” “at what moment did he start,” “was he turning those screws fast or slow.”

Both kinds are called “visual understanding,” but their fates are completely different. Kind one has been beaten to saturation on public datasets — engineering-wise it’s deliverable today. Kind two is the entire industry’s capability boundary in 2026 — the strongest closed models fail the pass line, and not in a “wait six months” way. This post walks through the state of both, where the boundary sits, what the correct architecture looks like, what the money math is, and where the open-source licensing traps are. Data verified as of October 2026; every benchmark score carries its caveats, because the water content here is higher than in most fields.
